source.title: 15. Management of Diabetes in Pregnancy: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026
source.organization: American Diabetes Association Professional Practice Committee for Diabetes

extraction_metadata.scope_note: The guideline chapter was treated as a secondary clinical-practice source. Numbered recommendations are represented as author_conclusion atoms tagged guideline_recommendation. Quantitative findings summarized from cited studies are tagged secondary_reported_result and remain anchored to this chapter rather than represented as primary-study findings. Bibliography entries were exported separately and not atomized.

atoms.canonical_statement: The chapter addresses management of preexisting type 1 or type 2 diabetes and gestational diabetes before, during, and after pregnancy, with emphasis on maternal and fetal risk reduction.

Diabetes in pregnancy is associated with maternal and fetal risks including spontaneous abortion, fetal anomalies, preeclampsia, fetal demise, macrosomia, neonatal hypoglycemia, neonatal hyperbilirubinemia, and neonatal respiratory distress syndrome.
Preconception counseling should be incorporated into routine diabetes care starting at puberty and continuing for all people with diabetes and childbearing potential.
Family planning should be discussed and effective contraception, including consideration of long-acting reversible contraception, should be used until treatment and A1C are optimized for pregnancy.

Preconception counseling should aim for glucose as close to normal as safely possible, ideally A1C below 6.5% (48 mmol/mol), to reduce congenital anomalies, preeclampsia, macrosomia, preterm birth, and other complications.

People with a history of gestational diabetes should seek preconception diabetes screening and care to identify and treat hyperglycemia and prevent congenital malformations and other adverse maternal and fetal outcomes.

People with preexisting diabetes who are planning pregnancy should ideally begin interprofessional preconception care that includes endocrinology, maternal-fetal medicine, nutrition, and diabetes education specialists when available.
Preconception care should include focused attention on achieving glycemic goals.
Standard preconception care should be augmented with extra focus on nutrition, physical activity, diabetes self-care education, and screening for diabetes comorbidities and complications.
People with preexisting diabetes planning or entering pregnancy should be counseled about the risk of developing or worsening diabetic retinopathy.

Dilated eye examination should occur ideally before pregnancy and in the first trimester, with monitoring every trimester and for 1 year postpartum according to retinopathy severity and eye-care recommendations.

In a randomized trial of people with overweight or obesity and prior gestational diabetes, prepregnancy weight loss of at least 5% was associated with lower gestational diabetes recurrence (OR 0.18, 95% CI 0.04–0.88).

population.label: People with overweight or obesity and a history of gestational diabetes

atoms.canonical_statement: Preconception glucose goals cited by the chapter are preprandial glucose 80–110 mg/dL and 2-hour postprandial glucose below 155 mg/dL; prandial insulin dose should be reduced for postprandial glucose below 100 mg/dL.

GLP-1 receptor agonists and dual GIP/GLP-1 receptor agonists should be stopped before pregnancy and contraception used during treatment; the chapter cites a 2-month preconception discontinuation interval for semaglutide and a 1-month interval for tirzepatide in Canadian prescribing information.

Table 15.1 preconception education includes nutrition assessment, lifestyle guidance, diabetes self-management education, counseling on pregnancy risks and diabetes physiology, and folic acid supplementation of 400–800 micrograms/day.
Table 15.1 health assessment includes overall health, diabetes comorbidities and complications, obstetric and gynecologic history, medication review, and pregnancy appropriateness of medications.

Table 15.1 screening includes diabetes complications and comorbidities, comprehensive foot and eye examinations, selected ECG evaluation, lipid panel, creatinine, TSH, urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio, anemia, genetic carrier status, and infectious disease screening.

Table 15.1 preconception planning includes immunizations, a nutrition and medication plan to reach glycemic goals using appropriate monitoring and technology, contraception until glycemic goals are achieved, and management plans for comorbidities and complications.

Fasting, preprandial, and postprandial glucose monitoring are recommended in diabetes in pregnancy, with goals fasting below 95 mg/dL, 1-hour postprandial below 140 mg/dL, or 2-hour postprandial below 120 mg/dL.
The ideal A1C goal in pregnancy is below 6% (42 mmol/mol) if achievable without significant hypoglycemia, and may be relaxed to below 7% (53 mmol/mol) when needed to prevent hypoglycemia.
CGM can help achieve time-in-range and time-above-range glycemic goals in type 1 diabetes and pregnancy.
CGM can help achieve the A1C goal in type 1 diabetes and pregnancy.
CGM may be beneficial for other types of diabetes in pregnancy.
CGM is recommended for pregnant people with type 1 diabetes.
When used with traditional pre- and postprandial glycemic goals, CGM can reduce large-for-gestational-age births and neonatal hypoglycemia in type 1 diabetes pregnancy.
CGM metrics may be used with blood glucose monitoring to achieve optimal pre- and postprandial glycemic goals.
Estimated A1C and glucose management indicator calculations should not be used as estimates of A1C during pregnancy.

For type 1 or type 2 diabetes in pregnancy, Table 15.2 lists fasting glucose 70–95 mg/dL, 1-hour postprandial glucose 110–140 mg/dL, and 2-hour postprandial glucose 100–120 mg/dL; less stringent goals are appropriate if necessary to avoid significant hypoglycemia.

atoms.canonical_statement: For insulin-treated gestational diabetes, Table 15.2 lists fasting glucose 70–95 mg/dL, 1-hour postprandial glucose 110–140 mg/dL, and 2-hour postprandial glucose 100–120 mg/dL.

source_anchor.sentence: Table 15.2, GDM treated with insulin column

atoms.canonical_statement: For gestational diabetes not treated with insulin, Table 15.2 lists fasting glucose below 95 mg/dL, 1-hour postprandial glucose below 140 mg/dL, and 2-hour postprandial glucose below 120 mg/dL.

source_anchor.sentence: Table 15.2, GDM not treated with insulin column

atoms.canonical_statement: For hyperglycemia less than overt diabetes detected early in pregnancy, treatment benefits remain uncertain, optimal management is controversial, and professional society guidance conflicts.

In TOBOGM, early treatment of gestational diabetes modestly improved the composite adverse neonatal outcome: 24.9% with early treatment versus 30.5% with control, relative risk 0.82 (95% CI 0.68–0.98).

population.label: Pregnant people with at least one hyperglycemia risk factor who met WHO criteria for gestational diabetes

concept.text: Repeat OGTT at 24–28 weeks with deferred treatment if indicated

atoms.canonical_statement: TOBOGM excluded people with fasting glucose 110–125 mg/dL (6.1–6.9 mmol/L), so the risk-benefit balance of early treatment in that subgroup was not evaluated.

For early abnormal glucose metabolism before 15 weeks, the chapter suggests nutrition counseling and periodic fasting glucose testing; testing and treatment may be intensified when fasting glucose is predominantly at least 110 mg/dL.

A1C should be a secondary measure of glycemia in pregnancy after glucose monitoring because pregnancy lowers A1C through increased red blood cell turnover and A1C may not capture postprandial hyperglycemia that drives macrosomia.

The CONCEPTT randomized trial found that real-time CGM added to standard care in pregnant people with type 1 diabetes modestly improved A1C and significantly improved maternal TIR and TAR without increasing hypoglycemia, while reducing large-for-gestational-age births, infant hospital stay, and severe neonatal hypoglycemia.

For pregnant people with type 1 diabetes using CGM, consensus targets are sensor glucose 63–140 mg/dL with TIR above 70%, TBR below 63 mg/dL under 4%, TBR below 54 mg/dL under 1%, and TAR above 140 mg/dL under 25%.
In one pregnancy CGM accuracy study, 20/20 agreement was 78.6% on sensor day 1, 96.3% on days 4 and 7, and 97.3% on day 10.

The chapter states that evidence is insufficient to support CGM for all people with type 2 diabetes or gestational diabetes, and pregnancy CGM metric targets for these populations are not yet defined.
Nutrition counseling before and during pregnancy should promote fruits, vegetables, legumes, whole grains, nuts, seeds, fish, other lean protein, balanced macronutrients, and healthy n-3 fatty acids.
Lifestyle behavior change is essential in gestational diabetes and may suffice for many people; insulin should be added when needed to reach glycemic goals.
Telehealth combined with in-person visits for gestational diabetes can improve outcomes compared with standard in-person care alone.
Insulin should be used to manage type 1 diabetes in pregnancy.
Insulin is the preferred agent for gestational diabetes.
Insulin is the preferred agent for type 2 diabetes in pregnancy.
Either multiple daily insulin injections or insulin pump technology can be used in pregnancy complicated by type 1 diabetes.
AID systems with pregnancy-specific glucose targets are recommended for pregnant people with type 1 diabetes.

AID systems without pregnancy-specific glucose targets or algorithms may be considered for selected pregnant people with type 1 diabetes when used with assistive techniques and experienced health care teams.
Metformin and glyburide should not be first-line agents for diabetes in pregnancy because both cross the placenta.
Metformin and glyburide may not be sufficient to achieve glycemic goals in pregnancy.
Other oral and noninsulin injectable glucose-lowering medications lack long-term safety data and are not recommended in pregnancy.
Metformin used for polycystic ovary syndrome and ovulation induction should be discontinued by the end of the first trimester.
The dietary reference intake cited for pregnancy is at least 175 g carbohydrate, 71 g protein, and 28 g fiber per day.
Studies cited by the chapter suggest that 70–85% of people diagnosed with gestational diabetes using Carpenter-Coustan criteria can manage it with lifestyle modification alone.
Regular exercise has been reported to reduce the odds of developing gestational diabetes by 38%.

population.label: Pregnant people

atoms.canonical_statement: Regular exercise has been reported to reduce the odds of gestational hypertension by 39%.

population.label: Pregnant people

atoms.canonical_statement: Regular exercise has been reported to reduce the odds of preeclampsia by 41%.

population.label: Pregnant people

atoms.canonical_statement: A meta-analysis of 32 randomized trials found that telehealth interventions combined with in-person care for gestational diabetes reduced cesarean delivery, premature rupture of membranes, pregnancy-induced hypertension or preeclampsia, preterm birth, neonatal asphyxia, and polyhydramnios compared with standard in-person care alone.

In type 1 diabetes pregnancy, insulin resistance begins increasing at about 16 weeks and total daily insulin dose rises by about 5% per week through week 36, usually resulting in approximately double the prepregnancy daily dose.
Observational studies cited by the chapter have not shown increased adverse fetal outcomes with insulin glargine compared with NPH insulin during pregnancy.
An RCT found insulin degludec noninferior to detemir during pregnancy, but the study was not powered for maternal safety or pregnancy outcomes.

Insulin degludec has a prolonged duration of at least 42 hours and a recommended 3–4-day interval between dose changes, which may impede rapid pregnancy titration and contribute to postpartum hypoglycemia when insulin needs fall sharply.
In the AiDAPT trial of 124 pregnant people with type 1 diabetes, AID increased TIR by 10.5 percentage points compared with standard care (P<0.001).

population.label: Pregnant people with type 1 diabetes

concept.text: CGM with multiple daily injections or standard pump therapy

atoms.canonical_statement: In AiDAPT, AID reduced TAR by 10.2 percentage points versus standard care (95% CI −13.8 to −6.6).

population.label: Pregnant people with type 1 diabetes

atoms.canonical_statement: In AiDAPT, AID lowered A1C by 0.31 percentage points versus standard care (95% CI −0.50 to −0.12).

population.label: Pregnant people with type 1 diabetes

atoms.canonical_statement: In an RCT of 95 pregnant people with type 1 diabetes, AID increased nocturnal TIR by 6.58 percentage points compared with standard care (P=0.003).

population.label: Pregnant people with type 1 diabetes

concept.text: Automated insulin delivery with 100 mg/dL target

atoms.canonical_statement: In the same 95-person RCT, AID reduced 24-hour TBR by 1.34 percentage points compared with standard care (P=0.002).

population.label: Pregnant people with type 1 diabetes

concept.text: Automated insulin delivery with 100 mg/dL target

atoms.canonical_statement: In the same 95-person RCT, AID reduced nocturnal TBR by 1.86 percentage points compared with standard care (P=0.0005).

population.label: Pregnant people with type 1 diabetes

concept.text: Automated insulin delivery with 100 mg/dL target

atoms.canonical_statement: An RCT of 70 people during labor and delivery found no difference between continuous subcutaneous insulin infusion and intravenous insulin infusion in neonatal hypoglycemia or reported secondary neonatal glucose outcomes.
Separate randomized trials cited by the chapter found inadequate glycemic outcomes with glyburide in 23% and metformin in 25–28% of participants with gestational diabetes.

Glyburide crosses the placenta, with umbilical cord plasma concentrations approximately 50–70% of maternal levels, and systematic reviews associate glyburide with more neonatal hypoglycemia and macrosomia than insulin or metformin.
Metformin monotherapy failure in gestational diabetes occurred in 14–46% of participants across systematic reviews and randomized trials cited by the chapter.

Long-term offspring safety remains a concern for placentally transferred noninsulin agents; metformin follow-up studies have produced mixed childhood anthropometric findings, and glyburide long-term offspring safety data are unavailable.
Pregnancy is a ketogenic state, and diabetic ketoacidosis can occur at lower glucose levels than outside pregnancy; the chapter states that DKA carries a high risk of stillbirth.
Recommended pregnancy weight gain is 15–25 lb for people with overweight and 10–20 lb for people with obesity; weight loss is not recommended because of small-for-gestational-age risk.
Pregnant people with type 1 or type 2 diabetes should receive low-dose aspirin 100–150 mg/day beginning at 12–16 weeks to lower preeclampsia risk.
Aspirin 162 mg/day may be an acceptable low-dose regimen for preeclampsia prevention in pregnant people with type 1 or type 2 diabetes.

The chapter states that data are insufficient to determine whether aspirin specifically reduces preeclampsia incidence in pregnant people with preexisting diabetes, despite benefit in high-risk groups overall.
For diabetes with chronic hypertension in pregnancy, treatment should be initiated or titrated using a blood pressure threshold below 140/90 mmHg to improve pregnancy outcomes.
Antihypertensive therapy should be deintensified if blood pressure falls below 90/60 mmHg during pregnancy.

Potentially harmful medications in pregnancy, including ACE inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers, and mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, should be stopped before conception and avoided in sexually active people of childbearing potential who are not using reliable contraception.

In most circumstances, lipid-lowering medications should be stopped before conception and avoided in sexually active people with diabetes and childbearing potential who are not using reliable contraception.

Lipid-lowering therapy may be continued during pregnancy in selected circumstances such as familial hypercholesterolemia, severe hypertriglyceridemia, or prior atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease when benefits outweigh risks.

In a secondary CHAP analysis of 434 people with diabetes and chronic hypertension, attained blood pressure below 130/80 mmHg was associated with a lower primary composite adverse perinatal outcome than 130–139/80–89 mmHg (19.3% vs 46.5%; adjusted RR 0.43, 95% CI 0.30–0.61).

population.label: Pregnant people with diabetes and chronic hypertension

atoms.canonical_statement: In the same CHAP secondary analysis, attained blood pressure below 130/80 mmHg was associated with less preeclampsia with severe features (14.0% vs 40.5%; adjusted RR 0.35, 95% CI 0.23–0.54; P<0.01).

population.label: Pregnant people with diabetes and chronic hypertension

atoms.canonical_statement: In the same CHAP secondary analysis, attained blood pressure below 130/80 mmHg was associated with less indicated preterm birth before 35 weeks (8.0% vs 20.1%; adjusted RR 0.44, 95% CI 0.24–0.79; P<0.01).

population.label: Pregnant people with diabetes and chronic hypertension

atoms.canonical_statement: In the same CHAP secondary analysis, attained blood pressure below 130/80 mmHg was associated with less NICU admission (36.0% vs 51.4%; adjusted RR 0.74, 95% CI 0.59–0.94; P=0.01).

population.label: Pregnant people with diabetes and chronic hypertension

atoms.canonical_statement: The lower-than-130/80 mmHg CHAP subgroup comparison was observational within the randomized trial rather than randomized to that blood pressure goal, so causal attribution to the lower attained pressure is uncertain.

ACE inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers are contraindicated later in pregnancy because of fetal renal dysplasia, oligohydramnios, pulmonary hypoplasia, and intrauterine growth restriction; the chapter advises stopping them before pregnancy or as soon as possible in the first trimester.

For most people, statins and other lipid-lowering medications should be avoided during pregnancy, but selected high-risk patients may be considered for statin therapy through shared decision-making because observed teratogenic risk appears low while data remain limited.
In one study, immediate postpartum insulin requirements were roughly 34% lower than prepregnancy requirements.

population.label: People requiring insulin after delivery

atoms.canonical_statement: Insulin requirements should be evaluated and adjusted after delivery because insulin resistance decreases dramatically immediately postpartum.
A contraceptive plan should be discussed and implemented with all people with diabetes of childbearing potential.
Breastfeeding efforts are recommended for all people with diabetes.
Breastfeeding is recommended for people with a history of gestational diabetes for multiple benefits.
Breastfeeding after gestational diabetes is recommended in part because it is associated with reduced later type 2 diabetes risk.
Postpartum care should include psychosocial assessment and support for self-care.
People with recent gestational diabetes should be screened at 4–12 weeks postpartum using a 75-g OGTT and appropriate nonpregnancy diagnostic criteria.
People with a history of gestational diabetes should receive lifelong screening for type 2 diabetes or prediabetes every 1–3 years.
People with overweight or obesity, prior gestational diabetes, and prediabetes should receive intensive lifestyle intervention and/or metformin to prevent diabetes.
A synthesis of systematic reviews reported an association between breastfeeding and lower asthma or wheezing risk in children and adolescents aged 5–18 years (OR 0.91, 95% CI 0.85–0.98).

population.label: Children and adolescents aged 5–18 years

atoms.canonical_statement: The same synthesis reported breastfeeding was associated with lower maternal breast cancer risk (OR 0.81, 95% CI 0.77–0.86).

population.label: Mothers included in systematic reviews and meta-analyses

atoms.canonical_statement: The same synthesis reported breastfeeding was associated with lower maternal ovarian cancer risk (OR 0.70, 95% CI 0.64–0.75).

population.label: Mothers included in systematic reviews and meta-analyses

atoms.canonical_statement: The same synthesis reported breastfeeding was associated with lower maternal type 2 diabetes risk (OR 0.68, 95% CI 0.57–0.82).

population.label: Mothers included in systematic reviews and meta-analyses

atoms.canonical_statement: The chapter prefers the 75-g OGTT over A1C at 4–12 weeks postpartum because A1C can remain lowered by pregnancy-related red cell turnover and blood loss and the OGTT is more sensitive for glucose intolerance.
In a retrospective postpartum study, an A1C threshold of 5.7% had 80% sensitivity for detecting a 2-hour 75-g OGTT glucose value at least 200 mg/dL.

population.label: People with recent gestational diabetes who had both A1C and 2-hour 75-g OGTT testing

atoms.canonical_statement: In the same retrospective postpartum study, an A1C threshold of 5.7% had 80.8% specificity for detecting a 2-hour 75-g OGTT glucose value at least 200 mg/dL.

population.label: People with recent gestational diabetes who had both A1C and 2-hour 75-g OGTT testing

atoms.canonical_statement: The retrospective A1C postpartum screening study was susceptible to selection bias because only 677 of 9,118 people had both A1C and OGTT performed, a combination not routinely obtained unless diabetes concern is higher.

After gestational diabetes, lifetime maternal diabetes risk is estimated at 50–60%, and the chapter cites an approximately 10-fold higher risk of type 2 diabetes compared with people without gestational diabetes.
After gestational diabetes, absolute type 2 diabetes risk is described as rising approximately linearly to 20% at 10 years, 30% at 20 years, 40% at 30 years, 50% at 40 years, and 60% at 50 years.
The chapter reports that type 2 diabetes risk after gestational diabetes is 18% higher for each unit increase in BMI from prepregnancy BMI at follow-up.

population.label: People with a history of gestational diabetes

concept.text: One-unit increase in BMI from prepregnancy BMI

atoms.canonical_statement: Among people with prediabetes and prior gestational diabetes, the chapter states that treating five to six people with intensive lifestyle intervention or metformin prevents one diabetes case over 3 years.
In people with prediabetes and prior gestational diabetes, lifestyle intervention reduced progression to diabetes by 35% over 10 years compared with placebo.

population.label: People with prediabetes and a history of gestational diabetes

atoms.canonical_statement: In people with prediabetes and prior gestational diabetes, metformin reduced progression to diabetes by 40% over 10 years compared with placebo.

population.label: People with prediabetes and a history of gestational diabetes
